Humankind died out decades ago, leaving behind mere vestiges of its time on Earth. As time went by, nature reclaimed land all over. In this resurgent world, apes have kept evolving. They've been gathering in tribes, growing, mastering human items, and advancing in their quest for knowledge. As the leader of such a tribe, you need to guide it towards collective intelligence. After Us is a deck-building and resource management game featuring an original and intuitive combo system in which players are each leading a tribe of apes. Starting only with tamarins, they combine their cards each turn to collect resources and gather victory points, attracting new apes into their tribe along the way: powerful gorillas, resourceful orangutans, versatile chimpanzees, and wise mandrills. The first player to obtain 80 points prevails in the race to collective intelligence — and wins the game. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Game Objective Be the first player to 80 points to win. Game Play The game is divided into 3 phases: 1. Assembling the Tribe - reveal the top four cards in your desk and arrange them to line up the frames. Player gains the resources in the completed frames. Resources are gained from left to right, top to bottom. If the closed box contains an arrow, you must pay the resources on the left to gain the benefit on the right 2. Attracting new apes - choose from one of your four discs to declare which primate you would like to gain. 3 resources for a level 1 card and 6 for a level 2 card. Blue Flowers for Mandrill (ability: victory points) Orange Fruits for Orangutan (ability: energy) Black Seeds for Gorilla (ability: rage; see below for explanation) Any sources of the same type for Chimpanzee (ability: copying) Note that the primate's ability is not their only ability. It simply means it is their dominant ability. Gain the sources on the disc that you have chosen. Optional: Spend 2 resources of the same kind to also gain the bonuses of ONE of your NEIGHBORING players 3. Resting Discard played cards. Return disc to face down position. Others Rage Spending four rages will allow you to remove a card from your deck. This can be done any time HOWEVER the card in your line up will NOT be replaced. Player will immediately gain the rage bonus as depicted on the upper right corner of the card. On BGA, click on the rage icon on upper right corner of card to use rage. Tools There are 3 human tools that each players can activate once per round with the required resources. [Rating: 2/10] No interaction. Cards are bought blindly so I don't even know if we can call it a deckbuilding. The puzzle of rearranging your cards was fun the firsts rounds, but eventually, you play with 4 cards and you just maximize your outputs. Cards you buy gives you resources and points, so throwing away your starting card is the optimal strategy. Very limited replayability.

[Rating: 2/10] This is the worst deckbuilder I have ever played. Random card buys is a bad mechanic, but there's so much shit on cards it honestly wouldn't matter if you could pick what to buy

[Rating: 2/10] A low decision main mechanism that ruins any impact it may have by having too few restrictions. Atrocious and directionless deck building. Repetitive rounds that make your eyes glaze over.

[Rating: 2/10] Played once and I'm pretty sure I've seen everything the game had to offer. Very little strategic depth or deviation from standard deckbuilder formulas. Surely when designing a deckbuilder you'd ask yourself "Why would anyone play this over Dominion?", a question that isn't successfully answered here.

[Rating: 2/10] Played at Essen Spiel 2023.  No fun at all. Just a multiplayer solitaire game on which there is almost no planning or tactical decision. Just moving some cubes into VPs. And you have no idea what others are doing as everyone plays at the same time

[Rating: 2/10] The worst bg i have played recently...do you really play or does the game play itself? This is pure randomness, there is no interaction at all and no choices.

[Rating: 3/10] No interaction. You can play on your side, and not knowing what other are doing. Very cold game.

[Rating: 3/10] After Us is about simians inheriting the Earth. But less in an exciting way and more in a "forcibly tranquilized" way. This game is a total snooze.  Read my review here: https://spacebiff.com/2023/07/24/after-us/

[Rating: 3/10] weird game of rearranging cards to align some boxes to get resources or resource conversion effects not much of a game the theme is not really there race to 80 points mainly resource converting completely multiplayer solitaire (!), no interaction not that much agency, very luck-dependent (top deck 4 cards, buying cards only blind from top, ...) It's not really deck building. (!)  It's like the second part of "Furnace" (the rearranging industry cards and converting resources).  When playing it a few times, it's a fine little puzzle, but it gets old fast. Imagine you're doing a head-down puzzle 

[Rating: 3/10] Played at GenCon. The game is so flat for first 6-7 rounds. As others described it, there's no player interaction what-so-ever. No surprises, just gather and spend resources for points.

[Rating: 3/10] Yay, the arts pretty. Theres like 7 total pictures of monkeys on the cards so thats barely a plus. Sure, theres kind of combos, but they seem obvious and proceederal. Played this a few times and each time was pretty boring. Getting better cards and culling the weak ones does not even feel like a classic deck builder where your deck gets really powerful and can combo into itself... like yay, this card gives me an extra fruit and 2 extra VP...yawn. I feel bad for the people who were excited for this game, its not good.
